newsitem.title: CHINA: China wheat harvest estimates vary, imports low.
newsitem.headline: China wheat harvest estimates vary, imports low.

text.p: Estimates of China's 1997 wheat harvest by traders and grain industry experts varied widely on Wednesday, but most sources agreed the crop should be close to previous records.

A crop similar to 1996's, variously estimated at between 100 and 116 million tonnes, would keep China's wheat imports for the June 1997 to May 1998 marketing year to three million tonnes, a Western marketing source said.
Customs figures released on Tuesday show China imported 810,000 tonnes of wheat in the first five months of 1997, down by 74.8 percent compared with the same 1996 period.
Imports in May were 250,000, the figures show, up from 210,000 tonnes in April.
Sources said no wheat import quotas had been issued.
A Chinese trader who recently toured wheat growing areas said there were no surprises for this year's wheat harvest as conditions were little changed from 1996.
The marketer put the 1996 wheat crop at 101 million tonnes based on information he had from a variety of official sources, and said he expected this year's output to be similar.
Carryover stocks from 1995 into 1996 were high, and government procurement bureaux had bought about 50 percent of the 1996 crop, he said.
But farmers in some regions had received IOUs for their grain, he and another source in China said.
"The government can't afford to buy it (the grain) because they're paying around $16 a tonne above the international market price," he said.
This sort of subsidising would have to come to a halt before China could expect admission to the World Trade Organisation free trade club, he said.

Farmers in production areas such as Shandong province in the east were now releasing their wheat onto the market and depressing prices -- a reversal of the situation elsewhere, where prices strengthen on reduced stocks as the harvest nears.
Prices released on Wednesday by the National Oils and Grains Information Centre show wheat prices almost 14 percent lower in some parts of China than they were a year ago.

Trading sources discounted official Chinese media predictions of drought damage to crops, saying this was more likely to be hedging on the part of local and provincial authorities in case anything went wrong with the crop.

Weather Services Corporation's report on Wednesday on China wheat weather said the conditions for mature winter wheat were favourable in central China, with fair weather and some scattered showers predicted for the next couple of days.
"Everywhere you go there is water for the crops, even if it is brought to the fields on a donkey, so drought is not a problem," one of the sources said.
China's State Flood Control and Drought Relief Headquarters and the Ministry of Water Resources issued an urgent notice on Tuesday calling for drought relief measures in many parts of the country.

Since the beginning of June, many regions north of the Yangtze river had been plagued by high temperatures and little rainfall, while record high temperatures hit northern China and western parts of northeast China, the Xinhua news agency said.
The drought has caused damage to about 17.3 million hectares (44 million acres) of crops, 5.8 million hectares of which were hit by severe drought, the urgent notice said.
China said this week it estimated the summer grain harvest at a record 118 million tonnes, up 3.5 percent on 1996.
China reported a record harvest of 490 million tonnes last year and has said it hopes to repeat that output in 1997.
-- Shanghai Newsroom (8621) 6279-8544
